an3.61:1.1: This is the only occurrence of the phrase “sectarian tenet” (_titthāyatana_). | _Tittha_, literally “ford”, is a path to salvation, used as a term for a non-Buddhist “religion”. _Titthakara_ is a “religious founder” (literally “ford-maker”); _titthiya_ is a “monastic of (another) religion” (for example at [pli-tv-bu-vb-np22:1.2.5]()); _titthiyasāvaka_ is a “disciple of a monastic of (another) religion”. | _Āyatana_ here is literally “home ground”, the defining belief or “tenet” of a religious community.
an3.61:1.4: This view was held by Jains, and others such as Ājīvikas. The view that all experiences are caused by past kamma is consistently rejected in the Suttas (eg. [an3.61:2.1](), [mn101:2.5](). This is reflected in the later Theravada commentaries, which describe five interacting _niyāmas_, or systems of natural law: seasons (_utu_), genetics (_bīja_), moral or immoral deeds (_kamma_), mind (_citta_), and principles of the teaching (_dhamma_). Nonetheless, the view that all experiences are caused by kamma is extremely common among modern Buddhists, and is often heard even from learned scholars. This is a harmful misunderstanding, as it has led to discrimination against the poor and disabled in Buddhist countries. One point of confusion is that rebirth into a particular life is caused by kamma, so in that general sense, kamma is a necessary condition for having a life in which one can experience anything. But the feelings experienced in that life are caused by a variety of things, not necessarily by kamma. | Note the use of _purisapuggala_ (“individual person”) as a Jain idiom. See [mn35:10.7]() and note, and [sn22.22]() and notes.
an3.61:1.6: Also at [mn101:22.5](). | _Issara_ (“God Almighty”) is the personal deity who created the world ([dn24:2.14.1]()), characterized by his “lordship” and “sovereignty” rather than, as with _brahmā_, his immanent divinity. He rarely appears in pre-Buddhist texts, where the creator is usually said to be Brahmā or Pajāpatī. It seems that, like the Hebraic Yahweh, _issara_ was originally a polytheistic conception, appearing in plural as a generic term for heavenly “sovereigns” (Atharvaveda 7.102, 12.3.42), while the monotheistic sense “soveign overlord” also appears in the same text (11.4.1, 11.4.10, 19.6.4, 19.53.8). This became one of the terms exalting the unborn Self as “lord of all” (_sarveśvara_, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). The current Sutta refutes the key tenet of the monotheist Śvetāśvatara, who lived within a few centuries of the Buddha. He used Īśvara in the sense “Supreme Lord” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7), who was the creator of all (6.16), including pleasure and pain (1.2).
an3.61:2.2: For other refutations of this view, see [sn36.21:2.1]().
